blocks.body:
The equation $x^2 = -1$ has no real solution. Complex numbers add one, called $i$, and then insist that the usual rules of algebra keep working. What comes out is far more than a formal trick: complex numbers are points of the plane, and multiplying by a complex number rotates and scales the plane. Trigonometry becomes algebra, and the formula $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ ties the exponential function to circles.

In number theory the most famous function, the Riemann zeta function, takes a complex variable written $s = \sigma + it$. Its real part $\sigma$ controls size and its imaginary part $t$ controls oscillation, and the main conjectures about primes are statements about where in this plane the function vanishes.

blocks.title: Complex number
blocks.body:
A complex number is an expression $z = a + bi$ with $a, b$ real, added and multiplied by the usual rules of algebra together with $i^2 = -1$: $$(a + bi) + (c + di) = (a+c) + (b+d)i, \qquad (a+bi)(c+di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i.$$ The real part is $\mathrm{Re}\, z = a$, the imaginary part is $\mathrm{Im}\, z = b$, the conjugate is $\bar z = a - bi$, and the modulus is $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. We picture $z$ as the point $(a, b)$ of the plane.

The modulus is the distance from $0$ to $z$, and $|z - w|$ is the distance between $z$ and $w$.

blocks.title: Arithmetic and the conjugate
blocks.body: The conjugate does most of the routine work. A direct computation gives $z\bar z = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2$, which is real and positive unless $z = 0$. So every nonzero $z$ has an inverse, $1/z = \bar z / |z|^2$, and division is done by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom: $$\frac{2 + 3i}{1 - i} = \frac{(2+3i)(1+i)}{(1-i)(1+i)} = \frac{2 + 2i + 3i - 3}{2} = \frac{-1 + 5i}{2}.$$ Conjugation respects both operations: $\overline{z + w} = \bar z + \bar w$ and $\overline{zw} = \bar z\, \bar w$. Taking moduli, $|zw|^2 = zw\overline{zw} = z\bar z\, w \bar w$, so $|zw| = |z|\,|w|$. Two further facts are used constantly: $\mathrm{Re}\, z = (z + \bar z)/2$, and the triangle inequality $|z + w| \le |z| + |w|$, which says a side of a triangle is at most the sum of the other two.

blocks.title: Polar form: multiplication is rotation and scaling
blocks.body:
A point of the plane at distance $r$ from the origin and at angle $\theta$ from the positive real axis is $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$. Here $r = |z|$ and $\theta$ is an argument of $z$, defined only up to adding multiples of $2\pi$. Now multiply two numbers in this form. Using the angle addition formulas from [[trig]], $$\begin{aligned} (\cos\alpha + i\sin\alpha)(\cos\beta + i\sin\beta) &= (\cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta) + i(\sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta)\\ &= \cos(\alpha+\beta) + i\sin(\alpha+\beta). \end{aligned}$$ So multiplication multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments. Geometrically, multiplying every point of the plane by $w = \rho(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi)$ rotates the plane by $\varphi$ and scales it by $\rho$. Multiplying by $i$ is a quarter turn, and $i^2 = -1$ is a half turn; that is the whole mystery of $\sqrt{-1}$.

Repeating the multiplication rule gives de Moivre's formula: for every integer $n \ge 1$, $$(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta,$$ by induction on $n$.

blocks.title: The complex exponential
blocks.body:
For real $\theta$, define $$e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta,$$ and for $z = x + iy$ define $e^{z} = e^{x} e^{iy}$.

The point $e^{i\theta}$ goes once around the unit circle as $\theta$ runs from $0$ to $2\pi$; and the rule from the previous section says exactly that $e^{i\alpha} e^{i\beta} = e^{i(\alpha+\beta)}$, the law of exponents.

blocks.title: Why the exponential, and roots of unity
blocks.body:
Why call $\cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ an exponential? First, it obeys the law of exponents, as just shown. Second, it has the right derivative: differentiating in $\theta$ gives $-\sin\theta + i\cos\theta = i(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$, just as $\frac{d}{d\theta} e^{c\theta} = c\, e^{c\theta}$ with $c = i$. Third, if you know the power series of $e^x$, $\cos x$ and $\sin x$, substituting $x = i\theta$ into $\sum x^n/n!$ and separating even and odd powers gives exactly $\cos\theta + i\sin\theta$. All three viewpoints agree, which is why this definition is the only sensible one.

Every nonzero complex number can now be written $z = re^{i\theta}$, and products become $re^{i\theta}\cdot\rho e^{i\varphi} = r\rho\, e^{i(\theta+\varphi)}$. Setting $\theta = \pi$ gives $e^{i\pi} = -1$.

The solutions of $z^n = 1$ are the $n$ numbers $\omega^k = e^{2\pi i k/n}$, $k = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1$, where $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$: the vertices of a regular $n$-gon inscribed in the unit circle. For $n \ge 2$ they add up to zero, since $\omega \ne 1$ and $$1 + \omega + \cdots + \omega^{n-1} = \frac{\omega^n - 1}{\omega - 1} = 0.$$ These roots of unity, and their sums, are behind a great many olympiad identities.

blocks.title: Functions of a complex variable, and n to the power s
blocks.body:
A complex function assigns a complex number to each complex number (or to each point of some region). Since input and output are both points of the plane, we cannot draw the graph, but we can watch what the function does to shapes. For example, $z \mapsto z^2$ squares moduli and doubles arguments, so it wraps the upper half-plane once around the origin; $z \mapsto e^z$ sends the vertical line $\mathrm{Re}\, z = x$ to the circle of radius $e^x$, wrapping around infinitely often.

For a positive real number $n$ and a complex exponent $s = \sigma + it$, define $n^{s} = e^{s\log n}$, using the ordinary real logarithm of $n$. Then $$n^{-s} = e^{-\sigma\log n}\, e^{-it\log n} = n^{-\sigma}\, e^{-it\log n}, \qquad |n^{-s}| = n^{-\sigma}.$$ The real part $\sigma$ decides how big the term is; the imaginary part $t$ only spins it around a circle, at angular speed $\log n$. This is why the series $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n\ge1} n^{-s}$ converges absolutely exactly when $\sigma > 1$: its absolute values are those of the real series $\sum n^{-\sigma}$. For $\sigma \le 1$ the series stops converging; the zeta function still makes sense there, as a [[continuation]] of the series, and its behaviour is governed by how the rotating terms $e^{-it\log n}$ cancel. The Riemann hypothesis is the assertion that all the zeros of $\zeta$ in the strip $0 < \sigma < 1$ lie on the line $\sigma = \tfrac12$.

blocks.title: Using polar form
blocks.solution:
$1 + i$ has modulus $\sqrt 2$ and argument $\pi/4$, so $1 + i = \sqrt 2\, e^{i\pi/4}$. Then $$(1+i)^{10} = (\sqrt2)^{10} e^{10 i\pi/4} = 32\, e^{5\pi i/2} = 32\, e^{i\pi/2} = 32i.$$ (Check: $(1+i)^2 = 2i$, so $(1+i)^{10} = (2i)^5 = 32 i^5 = 32i$.)

For the second, $w\bar w = |w|^2$. With $w = (-1 + 5i)/2$ computed above, $|w|^2 = (1 + 25)/4 = 13/2$. Alternatively $|w| = |2+3i|/|1-i| = \sqrt{13}/\sqrt{2}$, which avoids computing $w$ at all.

blocks.title: Multiple-angle formulas
blocks.body: Express $\cos 3\theta$ and $\sin 3\theta$ as polynomials in $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$.
blocks.solution: Write $c = \cos\theta$ and $s = \sin\theta$. By de Moivre, $\cos 3\theta + i\sin 3\theta = (c + is)^3$. Expanding with the binomial theorem and $i^2 = -1$, $i^3 = -i$: $$(c + is)^3 = c^3 + 3c^2(is) + 3c(is)^2 + (is)^3 = (c^3 - 3cs^2) + i(3c^2 s - s^3).$$ Comparing real and imaginary parts, $\cos 3\theta = c^3 - 3cs^2$ and $\sin 3\theta = 3c^2 s - s^3$. Using $s^2 = 1 - c^2$ and $c^2 = 1 - s^2$, $$\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta, \qquad \sin 3\theta = 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta.$$

blocks.title: A product of sines
blocks.solution:
Let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$. The roots of $z^n - 1$ are $1, \omega, \ldots, \omega^{n-1}$, so $$z^n - 1 = (z-1)\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(z - \omega^k), \qquad\text{hence}\qquad \prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(z - \omega^k) = 1 + z + \cdots + z^{n-1}$$ for $z \ne 1$, and therefore for all $z$ (two polynomials that agree at infinitely many points are equal). Put $z = 1$: $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(1 - \omega^k) = n$. Take moduli.

For real $\varphi$, $1 - e^{i\varphi} = e^{i\varphi/2}\left(e^{-i\varphi/2} - e^{i\varphi/2}\right) = -2i\, e^{i\varphi/2}\sin(\varphi/2)$, so $|1 - e^{i\varphi}| = 2|\sin(\varphi/2)|$. With $\varphi = 2\pi k/n$ and $1 \le k \le n-1$, the angle $\varphi/2 = k\pi/n$ lies in $(0, \pi)$, where sine is positive. Hence $$\prod_{k=1}^{n-1} 2\sin\frac{k\pi}{n} = n,$$ which is the claim. For $n = 3$: $\sin 60^\circ \cdot \sin 120^\circ = \tfrac34 = 3/2^2$.

blocks.title: A seventh-root-of-unity identity
blocks.solution: Let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/7}$. The seven roots of unity add up to zero: $1 + \omega + \omega^2 + \cdots + \omega^6 = 0$. Take real parts. Since $\mathrm{Re}\,\omega^k = \cos(2\pi k/7)$ and $\cos(2\pi(7-k)/7) = \cos(2\pi k/7)$, the terms pair up: $$1 + 2\left(\cos\frac{2\pi}{7} + \cos\frac{4\pi}{7} + \cos\frac{6\pi}{7}\right) = 0.$$ Solving gives the identity. The same argument shows $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\cos(2\pi k/n) = -1$ for every $n \ge 2$.

blocks.body:
- The rule $\sqrt{ab} = \sqrt a\sqrt b$ fails for negative numbers: $\sqrt{-1}\cdot\sqrt{-1} = i\cdot i = -1$, not $\sqrt{(-1)(-1)} = 1$. Square roots of complex numbers come in pairs, and there is no choice of one that respects multiplication everywhere.
- The argument is only defined up to multiples of $2\pi$, so "$\arg(zw) = \arg z + \arg w$" holds only modulo $2\pi$.
- There is no ordering of complex numbers compatible with arithmetic: "$z < w$" has no meaning unless both are real. Compare moduli instead.
- $|z + w|$ is usually smaller than $|z| + |w|$; equality holds only when one of $z, w$ is a non-negative real multiple of the other (they point in the same direction, or one of them is $0$).
- For a base $b$ that is not a positive real number, $b^s$ needs a choice of logarithm and is in general multi-valued. In $n^{-s}$ the base $n$ is a positive integer and the real logarithm is used, so there is no ambiguity.

Complex numbers are the setting for [[holomorphic]] functions, which are the main tool for studying the zeta function and its relatives. Writing sound waves and periodic functions as sums of $e^{2\pi i n x}$ is [[fourier-poisson]]. The characteristic equation of a linear differential equation often has complex roots, and $e^{(a + bi)x}$ explains the oscillating solutions; see [[ode-linear]]. In plane geometry, complex coordinates turn rotations and similarities into multiplication; see [[analytic-geometry]]. At the far end, the [[hodge]] conjecture is a question about shapes defined by polynomial equations in complex variables.

2. Find all complex $z$ with $z^3 = 8i$, and plot them.
3. Show that if $|z| = 1$ then $\bar z = 1/z$, and deduce that $z + 1/z$ is real.
4. Express $\cos 4\theta$ as a polynomial in $\cos\theta$.
